title: Nepal floods: Race against time to find workers. | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Hopes are fading for a quick rescue operation as Nepali crews and foreign specialists race to find scores of workers feared trapped alive inside hydropower tunnels in Nepal, after thick mud buried the facilities during last week’sdevastating flash floods.

Around 900 workers are missing at various hydropower projects that run along the Trishuli River, which winds through multiple districts in the remote and mountainous area, the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said Thursday.

A local police chief in one of Nepal’s worst-hit districts warned on Thursday the likelihood of finding the workers alive was declining, but said “we are trying our best.”

It’s not clear how many of the missing workers were inside the deep and heavily reinforcedtunnels when the water hit.

It’s also unclear how many of the workers may be still alive, with search and rescue efforts complicated by poor weather, mud, and the loss of critical infrastructure like roads and bridges.

“Tunnels are filled with liquid like mud. It’s not possible to complete this task in two or three days. By observing the situation, I see this may not even be completed in three to four months,” Brigadier General Ujwal Rana, who is involved in the search-and-rescue efforts, said Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the tunnel rescue operations will only progress “once the mud dumped by the flood dries” and a “stable footing is established.”

The missing hydropower workers are among roughly 5,500 people who remain unaccounted for in Nepal and China after the disastrous flooding, which has killed more than 1,200 people, according to authorities.

Here’s what we know so far.

Last week, around 900 workers were initially reported as missing at various hydropower projects in the country’s north, according to Nepal’s Independent Power Producers’ Association (IPPAN).

That number was revised down to 639 late Monday by NDRRMA, the disaster authority, but raised again on Wednesday to around 900. Shah said earlier this week the number of missing people would continue to fluctuate amid the challenging rescue efforts.

Most of the workers reported as missing were at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydrowater Project that was under construction in the Rasuwa District, according to a list supplied by IPPAN.

The list includes 12 projects – eight operational hydropower stations and four under construction – in two districts that were affected by flooding.

Each project presents its own challenges to rescuers who are trying to find the safest way in. Some have internal tunnels stretching several kilometers, meaning any workers inside could be a long way from the portal.

Rooms and resources inside the tunnels could theoretically help any trapped workers to survive – potentially for weeks, though air supply could be another problem.

At the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant,where 42 people were listed as missing,a massive operation has been underway to bore into a tunnel so rescuers can search for survivors.

The tunnel that leads to the underground powerhouse there, where dozens of people were working when the flood hit, is more than four kilometers (2.5 miles) long.

Arnold Dix, a geologist in Australia who is advising rescuers at the Trishuli 3A plant, said Monday it wasn’t clear how much of the tunnel was filled with mud or water.

There are many other risk factors, said Dix. The turbine room could have filled with water if the emergency shutdown systems failed, potentially drowning anyone inside. And that water could potentially be released by the crews’ drilling, presenting a risk for rescuers. On Monday, workers blasted debris from the tunnel and set up a pump to drain water away.

Rescue efforts are also ongoing at Chilime Hydropower Plant, where at least six people are believed to be missing, Jenjen Lama, a mountain guide involved in the mission, told CNN this week.

Lama shared a diagram of the facility, which shows the 250-meter (820-foot) tunnel leading downhill before connecting with a larger facility including a service bay, control room, and the hydropower transformer.

Over the weekend, rescue teams found that the tunnel was “completely blocked by deep, muddy sediment and sludge,” which eventually reached up to their chests, said Lama. They only made it 130 meters into the tunnel before they had to stop; the damaged infrastructure also makes it hard for helicopters to land there, he said.

Inside the tunnel “there is the kitchen, there is some food … but I don’t know about the oxygen,” he said.

Meanwhile, at the Langtang Khola Hydropower Project, two bodies were recovered during a search operation, Rasuwa District’s police chief, Ashok Thapa, said Thursday.

“It’s already been eight days since the flood so rescuing them alive seems less likely,” Thapa told CNN. “But we are trying our best.”

Engineers and search-and-rescue teams from the Nepal Army and Nepali police were joined by specialists sent by India and China, who arrived over the weekend.

Teams used thermal camerason drones to search for survivors, while working to locate the entrance of the tunnels and clear away mud. At the same time, rescuers drilled holes through the top of the heavily fortified tunnels.

At the Trishuli 3A plant, rescuers managed to make a big enough hole that they could rappel inside using ropes and harnesses – but when they called out, they received no response.Earlier, they also pumped air into the tunnel and sent food inside.

But breaking through the top of the hydropower station presents its own difficulties. “We need special equipment to get through the steel and everything that’s surrounding the turbine room. So, it’s layer upon layer of technical difficulties,” Dix said.

Hundreds of hydropower workers have been rescued or managed to trudge their way out of the mud and silt riddled tunnels.

But those survivors, who each have harrowing stories of their own, are still searching for answers about their still missing friends, coworkers, and family members.

One such survivor, Bhakti Ram Bohara, estimated that only 100 people had made it out from his and other nearby projects, out of about 1,000 workers.

Among the missing was his brother-in-law. They had worked on the same team, spending weeks away from their families at a time, and sending money back to their home villages.

“His wife is my sister, and she is pregnant,” he told CNN on Sunday, breaking down into tears.

Another survivor, Ram Chandra, described gripping onto rungs of the ceiling to make his way out of the tunnel as water, concrete and debris swirled around him. He and his coworkers took six hours to reach the mouth of the tunnel.

Across Nepal, where more than 12,000 people have been rescued since the flooding, according to the NDRRMA, stories of survival are bringing hope.

The father of 5-year-old Manisha Magar, who was trapped in a collapsed building for 60 hours,described seeing footage of her being rescuedafter he thought he had lost her.

“She’s my child. That’s all I can say,” Lok Bahadur Uchai Magar told CNN’s Will Ripley, wiping away tears.

Nepal and its superpower neighbors – China and India – have invested heavily inhydropower projects across the Himalayasin recent years, hoping to harness the vast energy potential of its raging rivers.

The country’s power grid runsalmost exclusively on hydropower, with renewable energy sources accounting for 100% of its electricity generation since 2015.

The devastation could be a reality check for governments driving a boom in dams, tunnels, highways, railways and bridges across the Himalayas – with China leading the charge.

India, and to a lesser extent Nepal, havebeen on an infrastructure-building spreein recent years, funneling hundreds of millions of dollars into developments in a region that is acutely vulnerable to natural hazards and climate change.

Despite being one of the most ecologically and seismically sensitive areas in the world, the potential to tame its rivers into major hydropower projects has long enticed engineers. Demand for electricity with the development of AI could see efforts to harness the region’s rivers intensify.

Experts say the severity of the event and its positioning on the Nepal-China border should make state planners think more carefully about how they design, situate and scale projects in the region – and spark regional discussion about shared risk monitoring systems.

This story has been updated with additional developments Thursday.

CNN’s Simone McCarthy, Lex Harvey and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting

CNN’s Simone McCarthy, Lex Harvey and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting
